entries.7c40d23cf0c75bfb767fa980e168145cce25c69b: <div sID="gen11468" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="59" osisID="Ps.59" sID="Ps.59"/> <div eID="gen11468" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11469" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen11470" type="x-p"/> This psalm is of the same nature and scope with six or seven foregoing psalms; they are all filled with David's complaints of the malice of his enemies and of their cursed and cruel designs against him, his prayers and prophecies against them, and his comfort and confidence in God as his God. The first is the language of nature, and may be allowed; the second of a prophetical spirit, looking forward to Christ and the enemies of his kingdom, and therefore not to be drawn into a precedent; the third of grace and a most holy faith, which ought to be imitated by every one of us. In this psalm, I. He prays to God to defend and deliver him from his enemies, representing them as very bad men, barbarous, malicious, and atheistical, <reference osisRef="Ps.59.1-Ps.59.7">ver. 1-7</reference>. II. He foresees and foretels the destruction of his enemies, which he would give to God the glory of, <reference osisRef="Ps.59.8-Ps.59.17">ver. 8-17</reference>. As far as it appears that any of the particular enemies of God's people fall under these characters, we may, in singing this psalm, read their doom and foresee their ruin.
entries.a516183a07af20cca0f967dc993e49e6f1c0eccf: <div eID="gen11470" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen11469" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Prayer for Deliverance.</title> <div sID="gen11471" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Deliver me from mine enemies, O my God: defend me from them that rise up against me. <hi type="super">2</hi> Deliver me from the workers of iniquity, and save me from bloody men. <hi type="super">3</hi> For, lo, they lie in wait for my soul: the mighty are gathered against me; not <hi type="italic">for</hi> my transgression, nor <hi type="italic">for</hi> my sin, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">4</hi> They run and prepare themselves without <hi type="italic">my</hi> fault: awake to help me, and behold. 5 Thou therefore, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> God of hosts, the God of Israel, awake to visit all the heathen: be not merciful to any wicked transgressors. Selah. <hi type="super">6</hi> They return at evening: they make a noise like a dog, and go round about the city. <hi type="super">7</hi> Behold, they belch out with their mouth: swords <hi type="italic">are</hi> in their lips: for who, <hi type="italic">say they,</hi> doth hear? <div eID="gen11471" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11472" type="x-p"/> The title of this psalm acquaints us particularly with the occasion on which it was penned; it was when Saul sent a party of his guards to beset David's house in the night, that they might seize him and kill him; we have the story <reference osisRef="1Sam.19.11">1 Sam. xix. 11</reference>. It was when his hostilities against David were newly begun, and he had but just before narrowly escaped Saul's javelin. These first eruptions of Saul's malice could not but put David into disorder and be both grievous and terrifying, and yet he kept up his communion with God, and such a composure of mind as that he was never out of frame for prayer and praises; happy are those whose intercourse with heaven is not intercepted nor broken in upon by their cares, or griefs, or fears, or any of the hurries (whether outward or inward) of an afflicted state. In these verses, <div eID="gen11472" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11473" type="x-p"/> I. David prays to be delivered out of the hands of his enemies, and that their cruel designs against him might be defeated (<reference osisRef="Ps.59.1-Ps.59.2">v. 1, 2</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Deliver me from my enemies, O my God!</hi> thou art <hi type="italic">God,</hi> and canst deliver me, <hi type="italic">my</hi> God, under whose protection I have put myself; and thou hast promised me to be a God all-sufficient, and therefore, in honour and faithfulness, thou wilt deliver me. Set me on high out of the reach of the power and malice of those that rise up against me, and above the fear of it. Let me be safe, and see myself so, safe and easy, safe and satisfied. O deliver me! and save me." He cries out as one ready to perish, and that had his eye to God only for salvation and deliverance. He prays (<reference osisRef="Ps.59.4">v. 4</reference>), "<hi type="italic">Awake to help me,</hi> take cognizance of my case, behold that with an eye of pity, and exert thy power for my relief." Thus the disciples, in the storm, awoke Christ, saying, <hi type="italic">Master, save us, we perish.</hi> And thus earnestly should we pray daily to be defended and delivered form our spiritual enemies, the temptations of Satan, and the corruptions of our own hearts, which war against our spiritual life. <div eID="gen11473" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11474" type="x-p"/> II. He pleads for deliverance. Our God gives us leave not only to pray, but to plead with him, to order our cause before him and to fill our mouth with arguments, not to move him, but to move ourselves. David does so here. <div eID="gen11474" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11475" type="x-p"/> 1. He pleads the bad character of his enemies. They are <hi type="italic">workers of iniquity,</hi> and therefore not only his enemies, but God's enemies; they are <hi type="italic">bloody men,</hi> and therefore not only his enemies, but enemies to all mankind. "Lord, let not the workers of iniquity prevail against one that is a worker of righteousness, nor bloody men against a merciful man." <div eID="gen11475" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11476" type="x-p"/> 2. He pleads their malice against him, and the imminent danger he was in from them, <reference osisRef="Ps.59.3">v. 3</reference>. "Their spite is great; they aim at my soul, my life, my better part. They are subtle and very politic: <hi type="italic">They lie in wait,</hi> taking an opportunity to do me a mischief. They are all mighty, men of honour and estates, and interest in court and country. They are in a confederacy; they are united by league, and actually <hi type="italic">gathered</hi> together <hi type="italic">against me,</hi> combined both in consultation and action. They are very ingenious in their contrivances, and very industrious in the prosecution of them (<reference osisRef="Ps.59.4">v. 4</reference>): <hi type="italic">They run and prepare themselves,</hi> with the utmost speed and fury, to do me a mischief." He takes particular notice of the brutish conduct of the messengers that Saul sent to take him (<reference osisRef="Ps.59.6">v. 6</reference>): "<hi type="italic">They return at evening</hi> from the posts assigned them in the day, to apply themselves to their works of darkness (their night-work, which may well be their day-shame), and then <hi type="italic">they make a noise like a hound</hi> in pursuit of the hare." Thus did David's enemies, when they came to take him, raise an out cry against him as a rebel, and traitor, a man not fit to live; with this clamour they went <hi type="italic">round about the city,</hi> to bring a bad reputation upon David, if possible to set the mob against him, at least to prevent their being incensed against them, which otherwise they had reason to fear they would be, so much was David their darling. Thus the persecutors of our Lord Jesus, who are compared to dogs (<reference osisRef="Ps.22.16">Ps. xxii. 16</reference>), ran him down with noise; for else they could not have taken him, at least <hi type="italic">not on the feast-day, for there would have been an uproar among the people. They belch out with their mouth</hi> the malice that boils in their hearts, <reference osisRef="Ps.59.7">v. 7</reference>. <hi type="italic">Swords are in their lips;</hi> that is, reproaches that wound my heart with grief (<reference osisRef="Ps.42.10">Ps. xlii. 10</reference>), and slanders that stab and wound my reputation. They were continually suggesting that which drew and whetted Saul's sword against him, and the fault is laid upon the false accusers. The sword perhaps would not have been in Saul's hand if it had not been first in their lips. <div eID="gen11476" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11477" type="x-p"/> 3. He pleads his own innocency, not as to God (he was never backward to own himself guilty before him), but as to his persecutors; what they charged him with was utterly false, nor had he ever said or done any thing to deserve such treatment from them (<reference osisRef="Ps.59.3">v. 3</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Not for my transgression, nor for my sin, O Lord!</hi> thou knowest, who knowest all things." And again (<reference osisRef="Ps.59.4">v. 4</reference>), <hi type="italic">without my fault.</hi> Note, (1.) The innocency of the godly will not secure them from the malignity of the wicked. Those that are harmless like doves, yet, for Christ's sake, are hated of all men, as if they were noxious like serpents, and obnoxious accordingly. (2.) Though our innocency will not secure us from troubles, yet it will greatly support and comfort us under our troubles. The testimony of our conscience for us that we have behaved ourselves well towards those that behave themselves ill towards us will be very much our rejoicing in the day of evil. (3.) If we are conscious to ourselves of our innocency, we may with humble confidence appeal to God and beg of him to plead our injured cause, which he will do in due time. <div eID="gen11477" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11478" type="x-p"/> 4. He pleads that his enemies were profane and atheistical, and bolstered themselves up in their enmity to David, with the contempt of God: <hi type="italic">For who,</hi> say they, <hi type="italic">doth hear?</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.59.7">v. 7</reference>. Not God himself, <reference osisRef="Ps.10.11">Ps. x. 11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.94.7">xciv. 7</reference>. Note, It is not strange if those regard not what they say who have made themselves believe that God regards not what they say. <div eID="gen11478" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11479" type="x-p"/> III. He refers himself and his cause to the just judgment of God, <reference osisRef="Ps.59.5">v. 5</reference>. "The Lord, the Judge, be Judge between me and my persecutors." In this appeal to God he has an eye to him as <hi type="italic">the Lord of hosts,</hi> that has power to execute judgment, having all creatures, even hosts of angels, at his command; he views him also as <hi type="italic">the God of Israel,</hi> to whom he was, in a peculiar manner, King and Judge, not doubting that he would appear on the behalf of those that were upright, that were Israelites indeed. When Saul's hosts persecuted him, he had recourse to God as <hi type="italic">the Lord of all hosts;</hi> when those maligned him who in spirit were strangers to the commonwealth of Israel he had recourse to God as <hi type="italic">the God of Israel.</hi> He desires (that is, he is very sure) that God will <hi type="italic">awake to visit all the nations,</hi> will make an early and exact enquiry into the controversies and quarrels that are among the children of men; there will be a day of visitation (<reference osisRef="Isa.10.3">Isa. x. 3</reference>), and to that day David refers himself, with this solemn appeal, <hi type="italic">Be not merciful to any wicked transgressors. Selah—Mark that.</hi> 1. If David had been conscious to himself that he was a wicked transgressor, he would not have expected to find mercy; but, as to his enemies, he would say he was no transgressor at all (<reference osisRef="Ps.59.3-Ps.59.4">v. 3, 4</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Not for my transgression,</hi> and therefore thou wilt appear for me." As to God, he could say he was no <hi type="italic">wicked</hi> transgressor; for, though he had transgressed, he was a penitent transgressor, and did not obstinately persist in what he had done amiss. 2. He knew his enemies were wicked transgressors, wilful, malicious, and hardened in their transgressions both against God and man, and therefore he sues for justice against them, judgment without mercy. Let not those expect to find mercy who never showed mercy, for such are wicked transgressors.
entries.734d7f215e7f536d771ea869e12b1d614ff6d003: <div eID="gen11479" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Confidence in God.</title> <div sID="gen11480" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">8</hi> But thou, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , shalt laugh at them; thou shalt have all the heathen in derision. <hi type="super">9</hi> <hi type="italic">Because of</hi> his strength will I wait upon thee: for God <hi type="italic">is</hi> my defence. <hi type="super">10</hi> The God of my mercy shall prevent me: God shall let me see <hi type="italic">my desire</hi> upon mine enemies. <hi type="super">11</hi> Slay them not, lest my people forget: scatter them by thy power; and bring them down, O Lord our shield. 12 <hi type="italic">For</hi> the sin of their mouth <hi type="italic">and</hi> the words of their lips let them even be taken in their pride: and for cursing and lying <hi type="italic">which</hi> they speak. <hi type="super">13</hi> Consume <hi type="italic">them</hi> in wrath, consume <hi type="italic">them,</hi> that they <hi type="italic">may</hi> not <hi type="italic">be:</hi> and let them know that God ruleth in Jacob unto the ends of the earth. Selah. <hi type="super">14</hi> And at evening let them return; <hi type="italic">and</hi> let them make a noise like a dog, and go round about the city. <hi type="super">15</hi> Let them wander up and down for meat, and grudge if they be not satisfied. <hi type="super">16</hi> But I will sing of thy power; yea, I will sing aloud of thy mercy in the morning: for thou hast been my defence and refuge in the day of my trouble. <hi type="super">17</hi> Unto thee, O my strength, will I sing: for God <hi type="italic">is</hi> my defence, <hi type="italic">and</hi> the God of my mercy. <div eID="gen11480" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11481" type="x-p"/> David here encourages himself, in reference to the threatening power of his enemies, with a pious resolution to wait upon God and a believing expectation that he should yet praise him. <div eID="gen11481" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11482" type="x-p"/> I. He resolves to wait upon God (<reference osisRef="Ps.59.9">v. 9</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Because of his strength</hi>" (either the strength of his enemies, the fear of which drove him to God, or because of God's strength, the hope of which drew him to God) "<hi type="italic">Will I wait upon thee,</hi> with a believing dependence upon thee and confidence in thee." It is our wisdom and duty, in times of danger and difficulty, to wait upon God; for he is our defence, our high place, in whom we shall be safe. He hopes, 1. That God will be to him a God of mercy (<reference osisRef="Ps.59.10">v. 10</reference>): "<hi type="italic">The God of my mercy shall prevent me</hi> with the blessings of his goodness and the gifts of his mercy, prevent my fears, prevent my prayers, and be better to me than my own expectations." It is very comfortable to us, in prayer, to eye God, not only as the God of mercy, but as the God of our mercy, the author of all good in us and the giver of all good to us. Whatever mercy there is in God, it is laid up for us, and is ready to be laid out upon us. Justly does the psalmist call God's mercy <hi type="italic">his mercy,</hi> for all the blessings of the new covenant are called <hi type="italic">the sure mercies of David</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.55.3">Isa. lv. 3</reference>); and they are <hi type="italic">sure to all the seed.</hi> 2. That he will be to his persecutors a God of vengeance. His expectation of this he expresses partly by way of prediction and partly by way of petition, which come all to one; for his prayer that it might be so amounts to a prophecy that it shall be so. Here are several things which he foretels concerning his enemies, or observers, that sought occasions against him and opportunity to do him a mischief, in all which he should see his desire, not a passionate or revengeful desire, but a believing desire upon them, <reference osisRef="Ps.59.10">v. 10</reference>. (1.) He foresees that God would expose them to scorn, as they had indeed made themselves ridiculous, <reference osisRef="Ps.59.8">v. 8</reference>. "They think <hi type="italic">God does not hear them,</hi> does not heed them; <hi type="italic">but thou, O Lord! shalt laugh at them</hi> for their folly, to think that he who planted the ear shall not hear, and <hi type="italic">thou shalt have</hi> not them only, but all such other heathenish people that live without God in the world, <hi type="italic">in derision.</hi>" Note, Atheists and persecutors are worthy to be laughed at and had in derision. See <reference osisRef="Ps.2.4">Ps. ii. 4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.1.26">Prov. i. 26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.37.22">Isa. xxxvii. 22</reference>. (2.) That God would make them standing monuments of his justice (<reference osisRef="Ps.59.11">v. 11</reference>): <hi type="italic">Slay them not;</hi> let them not be killed outright, <hi type="italic">lest my people forget.</hi> If the execution be soon done, the impressions of it will not be keep, and therefore will not be durable, but will quickly wear off. Swift destructions startle men for the present, but they are soon forgotten, for which reason he prays that this might be gradual: "<hi type="italic">Scatter them by thy power,</hi> and let them carry about with them, in their wanderings, such tokens of God's displeasure as may spread the notice of their punishment to all parts of the country." Thus Cain himself, though a murderer, was not slain, lest the vengeance should be forgotten, but was sentenced to be <hi type="italic">a fugitive and a vagabond.</hi> Note, When we think God's judgments come slowly upon sinners we must conclude that God has wise and holy ends in the gradual proceedings of his wrath. "So scatter them as that they may never again unite to do mischief, <hi type="italic">bring them down, O Lord, our shield!</hi>" If God has undertaken the protection of his people as their shield, he will doubtless humble and abase all those that fight against them. (3.) That they might be dealt with according to their deserts (<reference osisRef="Ps.59.12">v. 12</reference>): <hi type="italic">For the sin of their mouth, even for the words of their lips</hi> (for every word they speak has sin in it), <hi type="italic">let them</hi> for this <hi type="italic">be taken in their pride,</hi> even for their cursing others and themselves (a sin Saul was subject to, <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.28">1 Sam. xiv. 28, 44</reference>), and lying. Note, There is a great deal of malignity in tongue-sins, more than is commonly thought of. Note, further, Cursing, and lying, and speaking proudly, are some of the worst of the sins of the tongue; and that man is truly miserable whom God deals with according to the deserts of these, <hi type="italic">making his own tongue to fall on him.</hi> (4.) That God would glorify himself, as Israel's God and King, in their destruction (<reference osisRef="Ps.59.13">v. 13</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Consume them in wrath, consume them;</hi> that is, follow them with one judgment after another, till they be utterly ruined; let them be sensibly, but gradually wasted, that they themselves, while they are in the consuming, may know, and that the standers-by may likewise draw this inference form it, <hi type="italic">That God ruleth in Jacob unto the ends of the earth.</hi>" Saul and his party think to rule and carry all before them, but they shall be made to know that there is a higher than they, that there is one who does and will overrule them. The design of God's judgments is to convince men that the Lord reigns, that he fulfils his own counsels, gives law to all the creatures, and disposes all things to his own glory, so that the greatest of men are under his check, and he makes what use he pleases of them. He <hi type="italic">rules in Jacob;</hi> for there he keeps his court; there it is known, and his name is great. But he <hi type="italic">rules to the end of the earth;</hi> for all nations are within the territories of his kingdom. He <hi type="italic">rules to the ends of the earth,</hi> even over those that know him not, but he <hi type="italic">rules for Jacob</hi> (so it may be read); he has an eye to the good of his church in the government of the world; the administrations of that government, even to the ends of the earth, are <hi type="italic">for Jacob his servant's sake and for Israel's his elect,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.45.4">Isa. xlv. 4</reference>. (5.) That he would make their sin their punishment, <reference osisRef="Ps.59.14">v. 14</reference>, compare <reference osisRef="Ps.59.6">v. 6</reference>. Their sin was their hunting for David to make a prey of him; their punishment should be that they should be reduced to such extreme poverty that they should hunt about for meat to satisfy their hunger, and should miss of it as they missed of David. Thus they should be, not cut off at once, but scattered (<reference osisRef="Ps.59.11">v. 11</reference>), and gradually consumed (<reference osisRef="Ps.59.13">v. 13</reference>); those that die by famine die by inches, and feel themselves die, <reference osisRef="Lam.4.9">Lam. iv. 9</reference>. He foretels that they should be forced to beg their bread from door to door. [1.] That they should do it with the greatest regret and reluctancy imaginable. <hi type="italic">To beg they are ashamed</hi> (which makes it the greater punishment to them), and therefore they do it at evening, when it begins to be dark, that they may not be seen, at the time when other beasts of prey creep forth, <reference osisRef="Ps.104.20">Ps. civ. 20</reference>. [2.] That yet they should be very clamorous and loud in their complaints, which would proceed from a great indignation at their condition, which they cannot in the least degree reconcile themselves to: <hi type="italic">They shall make a noise like a dog.</hi> When they were in quest of David they made a noise like an angry dog snarling and barking; now, when they are in quest of meat, they shall make a noise like a hungry dog howling and wailing. Those that repent of their sins <hi type="italic">mourn,</hi> when in trouble, <hi type="italic">like doves;</hi> those whose hearts are hardened make a noise, when in trouble, like dogs, <hi type="italic">like a wild bull in a net, full of the fury of the Lord.</hi> See <reference osisRef="Hos.7.14">Hos. vii. 14</reference>, <hi type="italic">They have not cried unto me with their heart when they howled on their beds for corn and wine.</hi> [3.] That they should meet with little relief, but the hearts of people should be very much hardened towards them, so that they should <hi type="italic">go round about the city,</hi> and <hi type="italic">wander up and down for meat</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.59.15">v. 15</reference>), and should get nothing but by dint of importunity (according to our marginal reading, <hi type="italic">If they be not satisfied, they will tarry all night</hi>), so that what people do give them is not with good-will, but only to get rid of them, lest by their continual coming they weary them. [4.] That they should be insatiable, which is the greatest misery of all in a poor condition. <hi type="italic">They are greedy dogs which can never have enough</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.56.11">Isa. lvi. 11</reference>), and <hi type="italic">they grudge if they be not satisfied.</hi> A contented man, if he has not what he would have, yet does not grudge, does not quarrel with Providence, nor fret within himself; but those whose God is their belly, if that be not filled and its appetites gratified, fall out both with God and themselves. It is not poverty, but discontent, that makes a man unhappy. <div eID="gen11482" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11483" type="x-p"/> II. He expects to praise God, that God's providence would find him matter for praise and that God's grace would work in him a heart for praise, <reference osisRef="Ps.59.16-Ps.59.17">v. 16, 17</reference>. Observe, <div eID="gen11483" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11484" type="x-p"/> 1. What he would praise God for. (1.) He would praise his power and his mercy; both should be the subject-matter of his song. Power, without mercy, is to be dreaded; mercy, without power, is not what a man can expect much benefit from; but God's power by which he is able to help us, and his mercy by which he is inclined to help us, will justly be the everlasting praise of all the saints. (2.) He would praise him because he had, many a time, and all along, found him his defence and his refuge in the day of trouble. God brings his people into trouble, that they may experience his power and mercy in protecting and sheltering them, and may have occasion to praise him. (3.) He would praise him because he had still a dependence upon him and a confidence in him, as his strength to support him and carry him on in his duty, his defence to keep him safe from evil, and the God of his mercy to make him happy and easy. He that is all this to us is certainly worthy of our best affections, praises, and services. <div eID="gen11484" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11485" type="x-p"/> 2. How he would praise God. (1.) He would <hi type="italic">sing.</hi> As that is a natural expression of joy, so it is an instituted ordinance for the exerting and exciting of holy joy and thankfulness. (2.) He would <hi type="italic">sing aloud,</hi> as one much affected with the glory of God, that was not ashamed to own it, and that desired to affect others with it. He will sing of God's power, but he will sing aloud of his mercy; the consideration of that raises his affections more than any thing else. (3.) He would sing aloud <hi type="italic">in the morning,</hi> when his spirits were most fresh and lively. God's compassions are new every morning, and therefore it is fit to begin the day with his praises. (4.) He would <hi type="italic">sing unto God</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.59.17">v. 17</reference>), to his honour and glory, and with him in his eye. As we must direct our prayers to God, so to him we must direct our praises, and must look up, making melody to the Lord.  <chapter eID="Ps.59"/> <div eID="gen11485" type="x-p"/>

entries.788d777a772aaaa74f1fbd3d55ba62e1a7977fe1: <div eID="gen20522" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen20523" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen20524" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen20524" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen20523" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen20525" type="x-p"/> The psalmist prays for deliverance from his enemies, whose desperate wickedness he describes, <reference osisRef="Psa.59.1-Psa.59.7">Psa 59:1-7</reference>; professes strong confidence in God, <reference osisRef="Psa.59.8-Psa.59.10">Psa 59:8-10</reference>; speaks of the destruction of his enemies, <reference osisRef="Psa.59.11-Psa.59.15">Psa 59:11-15</reference>; praises God for benefits already received; and determines to trust in him, <reference osisRef="Psa.59.16">Psa 59:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.59.17">Psa 59:17</reference>. <div eID="gen20525" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20526" type="x-p"/> The title, "To the chief Musician, Al-taschith, Michtam of David," has already occurred: and perhaps means no more than that the present Psalm is to be sung as <reference osisRef="Psa.57.1-Psa.57.11">Psa 57:1-11</reference>, the first which bears this title. But there is here added the supposed occasion on which David made this Psalm: it was, "when Saul sent, and they watched the house to kill him." When the reader considers the whole of this Psalm carefully, he will be convinced that the title does not correspond to the contents. There is scarcely any thing in it that can apply to the circumstances of Saul's sending his guards by night to keep the avenues to the house of David, that when the morning came they might seize and slay him; and of his being saved through the information given him by his wife Michal, in consequence of which he was let down through a window, and so escaped. See <reference osisRef="1Sam.19.10">1Sam 19:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.19.11">1Sam 19:11</reference>. There is not in the whole Psalm any positive allusion to this history; and there are many things in it which show it to be utterly inconsistent with the facts of that history. The Psalm most evidently agrees to the time of Nehemiah, when he was endeavoring to rebuild the walls of Jerusalem, when the enterprise was first mocked; then opposed by Sanballat the Horonite, Tobiah the Ammonite, and Geshem the Arabian, who watched day and night that they might cause the work to cease; and laid ambuscades for the life of Nehemiah himself. Every part of the Psalm agrees to this: and I am therefore of Calmet's opinion, that the Psalm was composed in that time, and probably by Nehemiah, or by Esdras. <div eID="gen20526" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20527" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen20527" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20528" type="x-p"/> Deliver me from mine enernies, O my God - A very proper prayer in the mouth of Nehemiah, when resisted in his attempts to rebuild the walls of Jerusalem by Sanballat, Tobiah, and Geshem, who opposed the work, and endeavored to take away the life of the person whom God had raised up to restore and rebuild Jerusalem. I conceive the Psalm to have been made on this occasion; and on this hypothesis alone I think it capable of consistent explanation.
entries.c1e3dbcf236704cbe1e2e8e929171dba8e81847a: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen20528" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20529" type="x-p"/> The workers of iniquity - Principally Sanballat the Horonite, Tobiah the Ammonite, and Geshem the Arabian; who were the chief enemies of the poor returned captives. <div eID="gen20529" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20530" type="x-p"/> Bloody men - The above, who sought the destruction of the Israelites; and particularly, that of Nehemiah, whom four several times they endeavored to bring into an ambush, that they might take away his life. See <reference osisRef="Neh.6.1-Neh.6.4">Neh 6:1-4</reference>.
entries.859e8fcf6efcf990869438ea84455151a042487e: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen20530" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20531" type="x-p"/> For, lo, they lie in wait for my soul - For my life. See the passages referred to above.
entries.7ced8bb6b9f1e33f2c7d5b394d4ee6d05931aa6b: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen20531" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20532" type="x-p"/> They run and prepare themselves - They leave no stone unturned that they may effect my destruction and prevent the building.
entries.8856985fd0a3512870b12bcf7d7407910d97741f: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen20532" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20533" type="x-p"/> O Lord God of hosts - This was a proper view to take of God. when Israel, a handful of poor distressed captives were surrounded and oppressed by the heathen chiefs above mentioned, and their several tribes. But Jehovah God of hosts, was the God of Israel; and hence Israel had little to fear. <div eID="gen20533" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20534" type="x-p"/> Be not merciful to any wicked transgressors - Do not favor the cause of these wicked men. They are בגדי און bogedey aven, "changers of iniquity:" they go through the whole round of evil; find out and exercise themselves in all the varieties of transgression. How exactly does this apply to Nehemiah's foes! They sought, by open attack, wiles, flattery, foul speeches, fair speeches, threats, and ambuscades, to take away his life. Do not show them favor, that they may not succeed in their wicked designs. The prayer here is exactly the same in sentiment with that of Nehemiah, <reference osisRef="Neh.4.4">Neh 4:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Neh.4.5">Neh 4:5</reference>. Hear, our God, for we are despised; turn their reproach upon their own heads; - cover not their iniquity, "and let not their sin be blotted out."
entries.393ed733e374b5f0979e43155aa8c4e8f69a667c: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen20534" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20535" type="x-p"/> They return at evening - When the beasts of prey leave their dens, and go prowling about the cities and villages to get offal, and entrap domestic animals, these come about the city to see if they may get an entrance, destroy the work, and those engaged in it.
entries.e5c83ec05cd350bbc13f23e5bbf280fbd2cb12d1: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen20535" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20536" type="x-p"/> They belch out with their mouth - They use the lowest insult, the basest abuse. They deal in sarcasm, ridicule, slander, and lies.
entries.f40dc422901d3bd74c8bf104d0cdafae86fe2c6e: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen20536" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20537" type="x-p"/> Thou, O Lord, shalt laugh at them - They have mocked us; God will turn them and their schemes into ridicule and contempt: "Thou shalt have all these heathenish nations in derision."
entries.d8f1d0fa3c95285d7d1ab76bc66cd14241a60ba7: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen20537" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20538" type="x-p"/> Because of his strength will I wait upon thee - With this reading, I can make no sense of the passage. But instead of עזו uzzo, "his strength," עזי uzzi, "my strength," is the reading of fourteen of Kennicott's and De Rossi's MSS., of the Vulgate, Septuagint, Chaldee, and, in effect, of the Aethiopia, Syriac, and Arabic; and also of the Anglo-Saxon. To thee I commit all my strength; all I have I derive from thee, and all the good I possess I attribute to thee. The old Psalter translates, My strenght I shall kepe till the, for myn uptaker thou art. See on <reference osisRef="Psa.59.17">Psa 59:17</reference> (note).
entries.d0bd0cd635bc9a2ef8f1d28cd4de80ae9fbc6cdf: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen20538" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20539" type="x-p"/> The God of my mercy shall prevent me - The mercy of God shall go before me, and thus help me in all my doings. <div eID="gen20539" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20540" type="x-p"/> God shall let me see my desire - The sentence is short. God will let me see concerning my enemies, i.e., how he will treat them.
entries.9ab3d6c5e6c43d6157e4eb8fc550687a03ca50da: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen20540" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20541" type="x-p"/> Slay them not, lest my people forget - I believe the Chaldee gives the true sense of this verse: "Do not slay them suddenly, lest my people should forget. Drive them from their habitations by thy power, and reduce them to poverty by the loss of their property." Preserve them long in a state of chastisement that Israel may see thou hast undertaken for them: that thy hand is on the wicked for evil and on them for good. The Canaanites were not suddenly destroyed; they were left to be pricks in the eyes and thorns in the sides of the Israelites. It is in a sense somewhat similar that the words are used here.
entries.2ba89469865baf7d6720a261b72c5c6d18750d06: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen20541" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20542" type="x-p"/> For the sin of their mouth - This verse has puzzled all the commentators. If we take חטאת chattath for sin-offering instead of sin, we shall get a better sense. Some of Nehemiah's enemies made a profession of the Jewish religion. Tobiah and his son were allied by marriage to the Jews; for Eliashib the priest had married his grandson to the daughter of Sanballat; and this produced a connection with Tobiah, the fast friend of Sanballat. Besides this very priest had given Tobiah one of the great chambers in the house of the Lord, where formerly the meat-offerings, the frankincense, the vessels, and the tithe of the corn and wine and oil were kept; <reference osisRef="Neh.13.4">Neh 13:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Neh.13.5">Neh 13:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Neh.13.7-Neh.13.9">Neh 13:7-9</reference>. And there were children of Tobiah (probably the same family) who professed to be of the Levites, Nethinim, or children of Solomon's servants; but as they could not show their father's house and their seed, whether they were of Israel; these, and others which were children of the priests, were put out of the priesthood, and out of the sacred service, as polluted; as having sprung from intermarriages with heathens. See <reference osisRef="Ezr.2.59-Ezr.2.62">Ezr 2:59-62</reference>. Tobiah was expelled from the house of the Lord by Nehemiah, and all his household stuff thrown out of doors: <reference osisRef="Neh.13.7">Neh 13:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Neh.13.8">Neh 13:8</reference>. And this was doubtless one ground of the enmity of Tobiah to Nehemiah; and in this verse of the Psalm he may allude particularly to his occupancy of the chamber of offerings, which offerings, instead of being given to the Levites, were consumed by Tobiah and his household. This may be fairly gathered from <reference osisRef="Neh.13.6">Neh 13:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Neh.13.10">Neh 13:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Neh.13.11">Neh 13:11</reference>. Here then we have the sin of their mouth; their eating the offerings that belonged to the Levites; so that the temple service was deserted, the Levites being obliged to go and till the ground in order to obtain the means of life. And if we take חטאת chattath for sin-offering, it may refer to promises of sacrifice and offering which Tobiah and his family made, but never performed. They ate instead of offering them; and here was the sin of their mouth, in connection with the words of their lips, and their cursing and lying which they spake, for which the psalmist calls upon the Lord to consume them, that they may not be, <reference osisRef="Psa.59.13">Psa 59:13</reference>.
entries.65506937991714ace5a23e88eb0798378262c24d: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen20542" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20543" type="x-p"/> At evening let them return - He had mentioned before, <reference osisRef="Psa.59.6">Psa 59:6</reference> that these persons came like beasts of prey round the city striving to get in, that they might take possession. Now, being fully assured of God's protection and that they shall soon be made a public example, he says, Let them return and make a noise like a dog, etc., like dogs, jackals, and other famished creatures, who come howling about the city-walls for something to eat, and wander up and down for meat, grumbling because they are not satisfied, <reference osisRef="Psa.59.15">Psa 59:15</reference>. Nehemiah had made up all the breaches; and had the city guarded so well day and night, by watches who continually relieved each other, that there was no longer any fear of being taken by surprise: and now they must feel like the hungry beasts who were disappointed of their prey.
entries.640214b16222cd101544d319c266ccbe1db1e30c: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen20543" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20544" type="x-p"/> I will sing of thy power - For it was because thy hand was upon me for good, that I have thus succeeded in my enterprises. <div eID="gen20544" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20545" type="x-p"/> Yea, I will sing aloud of thy mercy - I shall publish abroad what thou hast done; and done not for my worthiness, nor for the worthiness of the people; but for thy own mercy's sake. <div eID="gen20545" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20546" type="x-p"/> In the day of my trouble - When I came with small means and feeble help, and had the force and fraud of many enemies to contend with, besides the corruption and unfaithfulness of my own people; thou wast then my defense; and in all attacks, whether open or covered, my sure refuge. I will, therefore, sing of thy mercy in the morning - I will hasten to acquit myself of a duty I owe to thee for such singular interpositions of mercy and power.
entries.e933e002de319c3bc04f9a7f37bfd7152c1c5288: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen20546" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20547" type="x-p"/> Unto thee, O my strength - A similar sentiment to that expressed, <reference osisRef="Psa.59.9">Psa 59:9</reference>. But the words are very emphatic: God is my strength; God is my elevation. My God is my mercy. I have nothing good but what I have from God. And all springs from his dwelling in me. God, therefore, shall have all the glory, both now and for ever. <div eID="gen20547" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20548" type="x-p"/> As many persons may still think that the inscription to this Psalm is correct, the following analysis may be applied in that way; or considered as containing a general resolution of the Psalm, without referring it to any particular occasion.  <chapter eID="Ps.59"/> <div eID="gen20548" type="x-p"/>

entries.e9153d2dabb179fc55f2083fc87223e451f273b8: <reference osisRef="Ps.59.1-Ps.59.9">Psa 59:1-9</reference> <div eID="gen9590" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9591" type="x-p"/> First part. As far as <reference osisRef="Ps.59.4">Psa 59:4</reference> we recognise strains familiar in the Psalms. The enemies are called מתקוממי as in <reference osisRef="Job.27.7">Job 27:7</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.17.7">Psa 17:7</reference>; עזּים as shameless, עזּי פנים or עזּי נפשׁ; as in <reference osisRef="Isa.56.11">Isa 56:11</reference>, on account of their bold shameless greediness, dogs. On לא in a subordinate clause, vid., Ewald, §286, <hi type="italic">g</hi>: without there being transgression or sin on my side, which might have caused it. The suffix (transgression on my part) is similar to Psa 18:24. בּליּ־עון (cf. <reference osisRef="Job.34.6">Job 34:6</reference>) is a similar adverbial collateral definition: without there existing any sin, which ought to be punished. The energetic future <hi type="italic">jeruzûn</hi> depicts those who servilely give effect to the king’s evil caprice; they run hither and thither as if attacking and put themselves in position. הכונן = התכונן, like the <hi type="italic">Hithpa</hi>. הכּסּה, <reference osisRef="Prov.26.26">Pro 26:26</reference>, the <hi type="italic">Hothpa</hi>. הכּבּס, Lev 13:55., and the Hithpa. נכּפּר, Deu 21:8. Surrounded by such a band of assassins, David is like one besieged, who sighs for succour; and he calls upon Jahve, who seems to be sleeping and inclined to abandon him, with that bold עוּרה לקראתי וּראה, to awake to meet him, i.e., to join him with His help like a relieving army, and to convince Himself from personal observation of the extreme danger in which His charge finds himself. The continuation was obliged to be expressed by ואתּה, because a special appeal to God interposes between עוּרה and הקיצה. In the emphatic “Thou,” however, after it has been once expressed, is implied the conditional character of the deliverance by the absolute One. And each of the divine names made use of in this lengthy invocation, which corresponds to the deep anxiety of the poet, is a challenge, so to speak, to the ability and willingness, the power and promise of God. The juxtaposition <hi type="italic">Jahve Elohim Tsebaoth</hi> (occurring, besides this instance, in <reference osisRef="Ps.80.5">Psa 80:5</reference>, 20; <reference osisRef="Ps.84.9">Psa 84:9</reference>), which is peculiar to the Elohimic Psalms, is to be explained by the consideration that <hi type="italic">Elohim</hi> had become a proper name like <hi type="italic">Jahve</hi>, and that the designation <hi type="italic">Jahve Tsebaoth</hi>, by the insertion of <hi type="italic">Elohim</hi> in accordance with the style of the Elohimic Psalms, is made still more imposing and solemn; and now צבאות is a genitive dependent not merely upon יהוה but upon יהוה אלהים (similar to <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.56.1">Psa 56:1</reference></hi>, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Isa.28.1">Isa 28:1</reference></hi>; <hi type="italic">Symbolae</hi>, p. 15). אלהי ישׂראל is in apposition to this threefold name of God. The poet evidently reckons himself as belonging to an Israel from which he excludes his enemies, viz., the true Israel which is in reality the people of God. Among the heathen, against whom the poet invokes God’s interposition, are included the heathen-minded in Israel; this at least is the view which brings about this extension of the prayer. Also in connection with the words און כּל־בּגדי the poet, in fact, has chiefly before his mind those who are immediately round about him and thus disposed. It is those who act treacherously from extreme moral nothingness and worthlessness (און <hi type="italic">genit. epexeg</hi>.). The music, as <hi type="italic">Sela</hi> directs, here becomes more boisterous; it gives intensity to the strong cry for the judgment of God; and the first unfolding of thought of this <hi type="italic">Michtam</hi> is here brought to a close. <div eID="gen9591" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9592" type="x-p"/> The second begins by again taking up the description of the movements of the enemy which was begun in <reference osisRef="Ps.59.4">Psa 59:4</reference>, Psa 59:5. We see at a glance how here <reference osisRef="Ps.59.7">Psa 59:7</reference> coincides with <reference osisRef="Ps.59.5">Psa 59:5</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Ps.59.8">Psa 59:8</reference> with <reference osisRef="Ps.59.4">Psa 59:4</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Ps.59.9">Psa 59:9</reference> with Psa 59:6. Hence the imprecatory rendering of the futures of <reference osisRef="Ps.59.7">Psa 59:7</reference> is not for a moment to be entertained. By day the emissaries of Saul do not venture to carry out their plot, and David naturally does not run into their hands. They therefore come back in the evening, and that evening after evening (cf. <reference osisRef="Job.24.14">Job 24:14</reference>); they snarl or howl like dogs (המה, used elsewhere of the growling of the bear and the cooing of the dove; it is distinct from נבח, Arab. <hi type="italic">nbb , nbḥ</hi>, to bark, and כלב, to yelp), because they do not want to betray themselves by loud barking, and still cannot altogether conceal their vexation and rage; and they go their rounds in the city (like סובב בּעיר, Sol 3:2, cf. <hi type="italic">supra</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.55.11">Psa 55:11</reference>), in order to cut off their victim from flight, and perhaps, what would be very welcome to them, to run against him in the darkness. The further description in <reference osisRef="Ps.59.8">Psa 59:8</reference> follows them on this patrol. What they belch out or foam out is to be inferred from the fact that swords are in their lips, which they, as it were, draw so soon as they merely move their lips. Their mouth overflows with murderous thoughts and with slanders concerning David, by which they justify their murderous greed to themselves as if there were no one, viz., no God, who heard it. But Jahve, from whom nothing, as with men, can be kept secret, laughs at them, just as He makes a mockery of all heathen, to whom this murderous band, which fears the light and in unworthy of the Israelitish name, is compared. This is the primary passage to <reference osisRef="Ps.37.13">Psa 37:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.2.4">Psa 2:4</reference>; for Ps 59 is perhaps the oldest of the Davidic Psalms that have come down to us, and therefore also the earliest monument of Israelitish poetry in which the divine name <hi type="italic">Jahve Tsebaoth</hi> occurs; and the chronicler, knowing that it was the time of Samuel and David that brought it into use, uses this name only in the life of David. Just as this strophe opened in <reference osisRef="Ps.59.7">Psa 59:7</reference> with a distich that recurs in <reference osisRef="Ps.59.15">Psa 59:15</reference>, so it also closes now in <reference osisRef="Ps.59.10">Psa 59:10</reference> with a distich that recurs below in v. 18, and that is to be amended according to the text of that passage. For all attempts to understand עזּי as being genuine prove its inaccuracy. With the old versions it has to be read עזּי; but as for the rest, אשׁמרה must be retained in accordance with the usual variation found in such refrains: my strength, Thee will I regard (<reference osisRef="1Sam.26.15">1Sa 26:15</reference>; observe, <reference osisRef="2Sam.11.16">2Sa 11:16</reference>), or upon Thee will I wait (cf. ל, <reference osisRef="Ps.130.6">Psa 130:6</reference>); i.e., in the consciousness of my own feebleness, tranquil and resigned, I will look for Thine interposition on my behalf.
entries.d993346f299195f401d32c9b333b95e5a1b9de33: <reference osisRef="Ps.59.10-Ps.59.17">Psa 59:10-17</reference> <div eID="gen9592" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9593" type="x-p"/> In this second half of the Psalm the cry of fear is hushed. Hope reigns, and anger burns more fiercely. The <hi type="italic">Kerî</hi> says that <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.59.11">Psa 59:11</reference></hi> is to be read: אלהי חסדּי יקדּמני, my gracious God will anticipate me, - but with what? This question altogether disappears if we retain the <hi type="italic">Chethîb</hi> and point אלהי הסדּו: my God will anticipate me with His mercy (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.21.4">Psa 21:4</reference>), i.e., will meet me bringing His mercy without any effort of mine. Even the old translators have felt that chcdw must belong to the verb as a second object. The lxx is perfectly correct in its rendering, ὁ Θεὸς μου τὸ ἔλεος αὐτοῦ προφθάσει με. The <hi type="italic">Kerî</hi> has come into existence in looking to v. 18, according to which it seems as though אלהי הסדּי ought to be added to the refrain, <reference osisRef="Ps.59.10">Psa 59:10</reference> (cf. a similar instance in <reference osisRef="Ps.42.6-Ps.42.7">Psa 42:6-7</reference>). But <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.59.11">Psa 59:11</reference></hi> would be stunted by doing this, and it accords with Biblical poetic usage that the refrain in v. 18 should be climactic in comparison with <reference osisRef="Ps.59.10">Psa 59:10</reference> (just as it also does not altogether harmonize in its first half); so that Olshausen’s proposal to close <reference osisRef="Ps.59.10">Psa 59:10</reference> with אלהי חסדי and to begin <reference osisRef="Ps.59.11">Psa 59:11</reference> with חסדו (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.79.8">Psa 79:8</reference>) is only just to be put on record. The prayer “slay them not” does not contradict the prayer that follows for their destruction. The poet wishes that those who lie in wait for him, before they are totally swept away, may remain for a season before the eyes of this people as an example of punishment. In accordance with this, הניעמו, by a comparison of the <hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>. in Num 32:13, and of the <hi type="italic">Kal</hi> in <reference osisRef="Ps.59.16">Psa 59:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.109.10">Psa 109:10</reference>, is to be rendered: cause them to wander about (Targum, cf. <hi type="italic">Genesis Rabba</hi>, ch. 38 <hi type="italic">init</hi>., טלטלמו); and in connection with בחילך one is involuntarily reminded of <reference osisRef="Ps.10.10">Psa 10:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.10.14">Psa 10:14</reference>, and is tempted to read בחלך or בחלך: cause them to wander about in adversity or wretchedness, = Arab. <hi type="italic">‛umr ḥâlik , vita caliginosa h. e. misera</hi>), and more especially since בחילך occurs nowhere else instead of בּזרעך or בּימינך. But the <hi type="italic">Jod</hi> in בחילך is unfavourable to this supposition; and since the martial apostrophe of God by “our shield” follows, the choice of the word is explained by the consideration that the poet conceives of the power of God as an army (<reference osisRef="Joel.2.25">Joe 2:25</reference>), and perhaps thinks directly of the heavenly host (<reference osisRef="Joel.3.11">Joe 3:11</reference>), over which the Lord of Hosts holds command (Hitzig). By means of this He is first of all to cause them to go astray (נע ונד, <reference osisRef="Gen.4.12">Gen 4:12</reference>), then utterly to cast them down (<reference osisRef="Ps.56.8">Psa 56:8</reference>). The Lord (אדני) is to do this, as truly as He is Israel’s shield against all the heathen and all pseudo-Israelites who have become as heathen. The first member of <reference osisRef="Ps.59.13">Psa 59:13</reference> is undoubtedly meant descriptively: “the sin of their mouth (the sin of the tongue) is the word of their lips” (with the dull-toned suffix <hi type="italic">mo</hi>, in the use of which Ps 59 associates itself with the Psalms of the time of Saul, <reference osisRef="Ps.56.1-Ps.56.13">Psa 56:1-13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.11.1-Ps.11.7">Psa 11:1-7</reference>, Psa 17:1-15, 22, 35, <reference osisRef="Ps.64.1-Ps.64.10">Psa 64:1-10</reference>). The combination ולילּכדוּ בגאונם, however, more readily suggests parallel passages like <reference osisRef="Prov.11.6">Pro 11:6</reference> than <reference osisRef="Prov.6.2">Pro 6:2</reference>; and moreover the מן of the expression וּמאלה וּמכּחשׁ, which is without example in connection with ספּר, and, taken as expressing the motive (Hupfeld), ought to be joined with some designations of the disposition of mind, is best explained as an appended statement of the reason for which they are to be ensnared, so that consequently יספּרוּ (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.69.27">Psa 69:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.64.6">Psa 64:6</reference>) is an attributive clause; nor is this contrary to the accentuation, if one admits the <hi type="italic">Munach</hi> to be a transformation of <hi type="italic">Mugrash</hi>. It is therefore to be rendered: “let them, then, be taken in their pride, and on account of the curse and deceit which they wilfully utter.” If, by virtue of the righteousness of the Ruler of the world, their sin has thus become their fall, then, after they have been as it were a warning example to Israel, God is utterly to remove them out of the way, in order that they (it is unnecessary to suppose any change of subject), while perishing, may perceive that Elohim is Ruler in Jacob (בּ, used elsewhere of the object, e.g., Mic 5:1, is here used of the place of dominion), and as in Jacob, so from thence unto the ends of the earth (ל like על, <reference osisRef="Ps.48.11">Psa 48:11</reference>) wields the sceptre. Just like the first group of the first part, this first group of the second part also closes with <hi type="italic">Sela</hi>. <div eID="gen9593" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9594" type="x-p"/> The second group opens like the second group in the first part, but with this exception, that here we read וישׁבוּ, which loosely connects it with what precedes, whereas there it is ישׁוּבוּ. The poet’s gaze is again turned towards his present straitened condition, and again the pack of dogs by which Saul is hunting him present themselves to his mind. המּה points towards an antithesis that follows, and which finds its expression in ואני. ויּלינוּ and לבּקר stand in direct contrast to one another, and in addition to this לערב has preceded. The reading of the lxx (Vulgate, Luther, [and authorized version]), καὶ γογγύσουσιν = ויּלּינוּ or ויּלּנוּ, is thereby proved to be erroneous. But if ויּלינוּ is the correct reading, then it follows that we have to take <reference osisRef="Ps.59.16">Psa 59:16</reference> not as foretelling what will take place, but as describing that which is present; so that consequently the <hi type="italic">fut. consec</hi>. (as is frequently the case apart from any historical connection) is only a consecutive continuation of ינוּעוּן (for which the <hi type="italic">Kerî</hi> has יניעוּן; the form that was required in <reference osisRef="Ps.59.12">Psa 59:12</reference>, but is inadmissible here): they wander up and down (נוּע as in <reference osisRef="Ps.109.10">Psa 109:10</reference>, cf. נוּד, <reference osisRef="Job.15.23">Job 15:23</reference>) to eat (that is to say, seeking after food); and if they are not satisfied, they pass the night, i.e., remain, eager for food and expecting it, over night on the spot. This interpretation is the most natural, the simplest, and the one that harmonizes best not only with the text before us (the punctuation ישׂבּעוּ, not ישׂבּעוּ, gives the member of the clause the impress of being a protasis), but also with the situation. The poet describes the activity of his enemies, and that by completing or retouching the picture of their comparison to dogs: he himself is the food or prey for which they are so eager, and which they would not willingly allow to escape them, and which they nevertheless cannot get within their grasp. Their morbid desire remains unsatisfied: he, however, in the morning, is able to sing of the power of God, which protects him, and exultantly to praise God’s loving-kindness, which satiates and satisfies him (<reference osisRef="Ps.90.14">Psa 90:14</reference>); for in the day of fear, which to him is now past, God was his inaccessible stronghold, his unapproachable asylum. To this God, then, even further the play of his harp shall be directed (אזמּרה), just as was his waiting or hoping (אשׁמרה, <reference osisRef="Ps.59.10">Psa 59:10</reference>). (In the Hebrew, v.1 is the designation 'To the leader:....A Psalm of David'; from then on v.1-12 in English translation corresponds to v.2-13 in the Hebrew)  <chapter eID="Ps.59"/> <div eID="gen9594" type="x-p"/>

PSALM 59
The title, which immediately follows, informs us upon what occasion this psalm was written, which bears a considerable resemblance to the preceding. He begins by insisting upon the injustice of that cruel hostility which his enemies showed to him, and which he had done nothing to deserve. His complaint is followed up by prayer to God for help; and afterwards, as his hopes revive in the exercise of devout meditation, he proceeds to prophesy their calamitous destruction. At the close, he engages to preserve a grateful remembrance of his deliverance, and to praise the goodness of God.
To the chief musician, Al-taschith, [destroy not,] Michtam of David,when Saul sent, and they watched the house to kill him.
The incident in David’s history, here referred to, is one with which we are all familiar, (1 Samuel 19:11.) Besieged in his own house by a troop of soldiers, and having no opportunity of egress from the city, every avenue to which was taken possession of by Saul’s guards, it seemed impossible that he could escape with his life. He was indebted instrumentally for his deliverance to the ingenuity of his wife, but it was from the divine goodness that he looked for safety. Michal may have contrived the artifice which deceived the soldiers sent by her father, but he never could have been saved except through the wonderful preservation of God. We are told in the words of the title that his house was watched, and this amounts, in the circumstances, to its being said that he was shut up to certain destruction; for the emissaries of Saul were sent with orders not only for his apprehension, but his death.
Psalm 59:1-5
1. Deliver me from mine enemies, O my God! lift me up from the reach of them that rise up against me. 2. Deliver me from the workers of iniquity, and save me from bloody men. 3. For, lo! they lie in wait for my soul: the mighty are gathered against me; not for my transgression, nor for my sin, O Jehovah: 4. They run and prepare themselves without my fault: awake to hasten for my help, and behold. 5. And thou, O Jehovah, God of Hosts! the God of Israel, awake to visit all the nations: be not merciful to any wicked transgressors. Selah.
 
1 Deliver me from mine enemies, O my God! He insists upon the strength and violence of his enemies, with the view of exciting his mind to greater fervor in the duty of prayer. These he describes as rising up against him, in which expression he alludes not simply to the audacity or fierceness of their assaults, but to the eminent superiority of power which they possessed; and yet he asks that he may be lifted up on high, as it were, above the reach of this over-swelling inundation. His language teaches us that we should believe in the ability of God to deliver us even upon occasions of emergency, when our enemies have an overwhelming advantage. In the verse which follows, while he expresses the extremity to which he was reduced, he adverts at the same time to the injustice and cruelty of his persecutors. Immediately afterwards, he connects the two grounds of his complaint together: on the one hand, his complete helplessness under the danger, and, on the other, the undeserved nature of the assaults from which he suffered. I have already repeatedly observed, that our confidence in our applications to a throne of grace will be proportional to the degree in which we are conscious of integrity; for we cannot fail to feel greater liberty in pleading a cause which, in such a case, is the cause of God himself. He is the vindicator of justice, the patron of the righteous cause everywhere, and those who oppress the innocent must necessarily rank themselves amongst his enemies. David accordingly founds his first plea upon his complete destitution of all earthly means of help, exposed as he was to plots on every side, and attacked by a formidable conspiracy. His second he rests upon a declaration of innocency. It may be true that afflictions are sent by God to his people as a chastisement for their sins, but, so far as Saul was concerned, David could justly exonerate himself from all blame, and takes this occasion of appealing to God on behalf of his integrity, which lay under suspicion from the base calumnies of men. They might pretend it, but he declares that they could charge him with no crime nor fault. Yet, groundless as their hostility was, he tells us that they ran, were unremitting in their activity, with no other view than to accomplish the ruin of their victim.

Thou shalt help me, and that seasonably, before it be too Late, and sooner than I expect.</ns0:note>: God shall let <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal 92. 11.</ns0:note> me see my desire <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">In their Disap<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pointment and overthrow, as it follows: Which was very de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sirable to <ns0:hi>David,</ns0:hi> no less for the publick good, than for his own Safety and Happiness.</ns0:note> upon <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> mine Observers.</ns0:note> mine enemies.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="11">11. <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">See <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 4. 14. 15.</ns0:note> Slay them not <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">To wit, suddenly, or at once.</ns0:note>, lest my people <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">My Countrey men; Or, those over whom thou hast appointed me to be Gover<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nour in due time.</ns0:note> for<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />get <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">Their former Danger, and thy glorious Mercy in delivering them, and their own Duty to thee for it. Hereby it most plainly appears, that <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> in those and the like Imprecations against his Enemies, was not moved there<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />unto by his private Malice, or desire of Revenge, but by the Respect which he had to God's Honour, and the general good of his People.</ns0:note>: scatter them <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Heb. <ns0:hi>make them to Wander.</ns0:hi> As they wandred about the City and Country to do me Mischief, v. 6. so let their Punishment be agreeable to their sin, let them wander from place to place, to wit, for Meat, as it is expres<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sed v. 15. that they may carry the Tokens of thy Justice, and their own Shame to all places where they come.</ns0:note> by thy power; and bring them down <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">From that Power and Dignity in which thou hast set them, which they do so wickedly abuse; and from the height of their Carnal Hopes and Confidences of Success against me.</ns0:note>, O LORD our shield.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="12">12. <ns0:hi>For</ns0:hi> the sin of their mouth, <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> the words of their lips <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">For their ungodly and injurlous, and pernicious Speeches, of which he speaks v. 7. and in many other places.</ns0:note>, let them even be taken <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">As in a snare in order to their Ruin. Let thy Judgments overtake them.</ns0:note> in their pride <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">For their proud and insolent Speeches against thee, v. 7.</ns0:note>: and for cursing and lying <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">For their Execrations and lying Reports, which they have raised or spread abroad concerning me.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:hi>which</ns0:hi> they speak <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Which they are ready to utter upon all Occasions.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="13">13. Consume <ns0:hi>them</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">By degrees; and after thou hast made them to wander a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bout, v. 11:</ns0:note>, in wrath, consume <ns0:hi>them,</ns0:hi> that they <ns0:hi>may</ns0:hi> not <ns0:hi>be</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">To wit, in the Land of the Living any more: As this Phrase is frequently understood; whereof divers instances have been given.</ns0:note>: and let them know <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Experimentally, and to their cost.</ns0:note> that God ruleth <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Over and above them: That though <ns0:hi>Saul</ns0:hi> be King, yet God is his Superior in Power and Authority, and all things among us shall be disposed, not as it pleaseth <ns0:hi>Saul,</ns0:hi> which his Parasites are always suggesting to him, but as God will; and therefore I shall be preserved, and in fit time Crowned, in spight of all that <ns0:hi>Saul</ns0:hi> or his Forces can do against me.</ns0:note> in Jacob <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">In the Land, and over the People of <ns0:hi>Israel,</ns0:hi> whose King and Governour he is in a peculiar manner.</ns0:note>, unto <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Or, and <ns0:hi>unto:</ns0:hi> The Conjunction, <ns0:hi>and,</ns0:hi> being oft understood, as hath been noted before. These words may be referred; Either, 1. To God's Ruling, let them know, <ns0:hi>that God Ruleth,</ns0:hi> not onely in <ns0:hi>Iacob:</ns0:hi> But also <ns0:hi>to the Ends of the Earth.</ns0:hi> Or, 2: To mens knowing, <ns0:hi>let them,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>let men know even to the Ends of the Earth, that God raleth in Iacob:</ns0:hi> Let thy Judgments be so manifest and dreadful in the Destruction of thy wicked Enemies, that not onely <ns0:hi>Israelites,</ns0:hi> but even the remote Nations of the World, may see it and ac<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />knowledge thy Power and Providence in it.</ns0:note> the ends of the earth <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Either of this Land: Or rather, of the World. The Sence is, That by those Eminent and extraordinary Discoveries of thy Power and Wisdom, and Justice, it may be Evident, both to them, and to all that hear of it, that thou art no Puny or Inferior, or Topical God, like the God's of Heathens, whose Government is confined to a narrow Compass, but the high and mighty God, and the great Ruler of the whole World.</ns0:note>, Selah.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="14">14. And at evening let them return, <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> let them make a noise like a dog, and go round about the city <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">What was their sin, and their choise to do with evil De<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sign, let it be their Punishment to do it by Constraint, and for Meat, as it follows, v. 15.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="15">15. Let them wander up and down <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> to Eat.</ns0:note> for meat <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">To get a Lively-hood.</ns0:note>; <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> if they be not satisfied, then they will stay all Night.</ns0:note> and grudg if they be not satisfied <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">When their Bodies are hungry, let their Minds be discontented. Or, as others render the Words, <ns0:hi>And lodge,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>be forced to Lodge all Night, when they are not satisfied,</ns0:hi> Let them go to their rest with an empty Stomach.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="16">16. But I will sing of thy power; yea, I will sing aloud of thy mercy in the morning: for thou hast been my defence and refuge in the day of my trouble.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="17">17. Unto thee <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">(<ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi>) To thy Honour. Or rather, <ns0:hi>of</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>concerning thee;</ns0:hi> as that Particle is sometimes used.</ns0:note>, O my strength, will I sing: for God is my defence, <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> the God of my mercy.</ns0:p>
